Wealth inequality is among the defining trends of the U.S. economy,
yet most research on how family wealth shapes children's development
relies on net worth, a single composite number that conceals the
distinct, sometimes opposing, roles of what families own and what
they owe. My research unpacks that composite.

My dissertation drew on longitudinal data following more than 7,000
young adults over 24 years (NLSY79 and its Child and Young Adult
cohort) to examine how parental assets and debts across three periods
of childhood relate to fifteen young adult outcomes spanning
education, economic wellbeing, mental health, behavior, and family
formation. Three findings anchor this work. First, assets and debts
are qualitatively distinct predictors, and treating them as a single net
figure obscures how each operates. Second, timing matters:
early-childhood wealth was linked to behavioral outcomes, middle
childhood to mental health, and adolescence to educational, economic,
and family formation outcomes. Third, young adults' own wealth
accumulation is a central pathway through which childhood economic
conditions carry forward — and assets and debts persist across
generations more strongly than net worth itself.

This work extends an earlier research program in health economics:
before studying wealth and child development, I spent a decade
examining how health, poverty, and inequality interact in transition
economies, in research supported by the Vienna Institute of
International Economic Studies and the Global Development Network and
in policy work with the World Bank, WHO, and the World Economic
Forum.

## Selected peer-reviewed publications

Miller, P., **Podvysotska, T.**, Jones, E., Hanson, J. L., &
Votruba-Drzal, E. (2026). How family assets and debts relate to
children's achievement and behavior problems across development.
*Social Development, 35*(1), e70033.
[doi:10.1111/sode.70033](https://doi.org/10.1111/sode.70033)

Miller, P., Elliott, L. E., **Podvysotska, T.**, Ptak, C., Duong, S.,
Fox, D., Coulanges, L., Libertus, M., Bachman, H. J., & Votruba-Drzal,
E. (2023). Toddler home math environment: Triangulating multi-method
assessments in a U.S. sample. *Frontiers in Psychology, 14*, 1105569.
[doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1105569](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1105569)

Miller, P., **Podvysotska, T.**, Betancur, L., & Votruba-Drzal, E.
(2021). Wealth and child development: Differences in associations by
family income and developmental stage. *RSF: The Russell Sage
Foundation Journal of the Social Sciences, 7*(3), 154–174.
[doi:10.7758/rsf.2021.7.3.07](https://doi.org/10.7758/rsf.2021.7.3.07)

*Earlier work in health economics, poverty, and inequality (published
under Podvysotska and Podvysotskaya) includes peer-reviewed articles
and working papers with wiiw, GDN, and DIW Berlin, and Ukraine's
National Competitiveness Reports (2012, 2013) produced with the World
Economic Forum. A complete list appears in my [CV](cv.qmd).*

## Selected presentations

**Podvysotska, T.** (2024, December). *Applying DDML (double/debiased
machine learning) in R and Stata: A use case from NLSY data on
parental wealth and children's developmental outcomes.* Invited
methods talk, CAMeL, Department of Psychology, University of
Pittsburgh.

**Podvysotska, T.**, Miller, P., Hanson, J., & Votruba-Drzal, E.
(2023, March). *Assets & debts and child development: Main effects
and developmental differences.* Paper presented at the SRCD Biennial
Meeting, Salt Lake City, UT.

Betancur, L., Miller, P., **Podvysotska, T.** (presenter), &
Votruba-Drzal, E. (2021, April). *The role of wealth components in
shaping children's academic and behavioral outcomes.* Paper presented
at the SRCD Biennial Meeting (virtual).
